architectural_implications.after: An instrumentation layer (OpenTelemetry/OpenInference) captures spans, token counts, model names, and tool calls, which evals then consume as input.
architectural_implications.before: Evaluation treated as an ad-hoc, end-of-pipeline check on final outputs, or as manual review of sample responses.
architectural_implications.consequence: Evaluation becomes a downstream consumer of a shared trace substrate, so instrumenting the agent is a prerequisite for any quality measurement, and evals can interrogate intermediate steps.
architectural_implications.observation: Tracing/observability must be established as a layer beneath evaluation, since evals consume trace data rather than raw application state.

architectural_implications.after: Prompt edits are treated as dependency-affecting changes that must pass a suite of evals covering unrelated behaviors.
architectural_implications.before: Changing a system prompt to fix a localized issue (e.g., tone) is assumed to be a contained edit.
architectural_implications.consequence: Prompt and agent codebases need a regression eval suite and CI gating, shifting prompt management from craft to engineering discipline.
architectural_implications.observation: Prompt changes become cross-cutting risks that can silently break unrelated behaviors, requiring regression coverage rather than point fixes.

architectural_implications.after: Each intermediate span (retrieval, reasoning, tool invocation, handoff) is inspected to find the true origin of cascading failure.
architectural_implications.before: Debugging centered on inspecting the agent's final response and guessing where it went wrong.
architectural_implications.consequence: Debugging and eval tooling must be span-aware, and multi-agent handoffs introduce an additional routing/triage failure surface that requires its own evaluation.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent failure localization moves from the final output to the span graph, because errors cascade across tool calls and reasoning steps.

source.author: AI Engineer
source.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Laurie Voss
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Evaluating and shipping production-ready AI agents using observability, tracing, code evaluations, LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, datasets, experiments, and meta-evaluation.
  • Purpose: To educate AI engineers on how to build, trace, evaluate, and systematically improve LLM-based AI agents using structured testing, evaluation rubrics, and observability tooling. Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, presents a comprehensive 101 workshop on moving AI agents from casual 'vibe checks' to reliable production systems. He explains why standard software unit tests and manual reviews fail for non-deterministic AI outputs, introducing a rigorous framework of OpenTelemetry tracing (via Arize AX), code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, golden datasets, error analysis, and meta-evaluation to iteratively improve agent prompts and codebases.

Topic Map

Introduction and Agenda

  • Explanation: Introduction of the speaker, background, and the core agenda covering evals, tracing in Arize AX, building AI agents with the Claude Agent SDK, error analysis, code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, meta-evaluation, and dataset/experiment iteration loops.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents make evaluation much harder than single-LLM applications due to cascading errors and multi-step tool calls.
    • Most teams ship AI features based on vague vibe checks, which fails when models encounter new inputs.
  • Examples:
    • Mention of building a financial analysis chatbot agent using the Claude Agent SDK.
  • Terminology:
    • Arize AX
    • Claude Agent SDK
    • evals
    • traces
    • spans
  • Why it matters: Establishes why traditional testing methods are insufficient for AI applications and sets the framework for the workshop.

What are Evals and Why You Need Them (The Vibes Problem)

  • Explanation: Discussion of the limitations of manual vibe checks and unit tests for LLM applications, explaining why traces are logs for AI and evals are tests for AI.
  • Key claims:
    • Traces are logs for AI; evals are tests for AI.
    • Without evals, changing a prompt to fix one tone issue can silently hallucinate product features elsewhere.
    • Manual human review does not scale, doesn't catch regressions, and doesn't run in CI.
  • Examples:
    • Changing system prompts and breaking unexpected parts of an application.
  • Terminology:
    • vibes problem
    • traces
    • spans
    • evals
    • regression test
  • Why it matters: Explains the foundational mental model needed to transition from prototyping to engineering production AI.

Two Types of Evals: Code Evals vs. LLM-as-a-Judge Evals

  • Explanation: Comparison of code-based deterministic checks versus semantic LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, highlighting their pros, cons, and appropriate use cases.
  • Key claims:
    • Code evals are deterministic, free, fast, and reproducible like unit tests, but can be brittle.
    • LLM-as-a-judge evals use a second LLM to grade outputs against a rubric, handling meaning and semantics rather than just strings.
    • LLM judges cost money, are non-deterministic, and require calibration against human judgment.
  • Examples:
    • Code eval checking if output parses as JSON or contains a ticker symbol.
    • LLM judge checking faithfulness or tone.
  • Terminology:
    • code evals
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • rubric
    • deterministic
  • Why it matters: Helps engineers choose the right evaluation mechanism depending on whether the test is syntactic or semantic.

Why Agents Make Evaluation Harder

  • Explanation: Analysis of multi-agent and multi-turn agent execution complexity, tool calls, and cascading errors.
  • Key claims:
    • Single LLM calls have simple input-output pairs, but agents make a series of tool calls and reasoning steps.
    • Errors cascade across steps: bad retrieval leads to bad reasoning, leading to confidently wrong output.
    • Multi-agent handoffs add another layer where triage and specialist routing can fail.
  • Examples:
    • Agent searching the web for Tesla, finding info on an 18th-century inventor instead, and writing a polished report about them.
  • Terminology:
    • cascading failures
    • multi-agent complexity
    • tool calls
    • hallucination
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates why monitoring intermediate agent steps (spans) is essential for debugging agent workflows.

Setting Up Tracing with Arize AX

  • Explanation: Demonstration of setting up OpenTelemetry tracing and OpenInference instrumentation with the Claude Agent SDK to capture raw data for evaluations.
  • Key claims:
    • You can't evaluate what you can't observe; observability comes before evaluation.
    • Auto-instrumentation via OpenInference captures prompt text, completions, token counts, model names, and tool invocations with just two lines of code.
  • Examples:
    • Code snippet registering tracer provider with Arize AX using space ID and API key.
  • Terminology:
    • OpenTelemetry
    • OpenInference
    • tracing
    • Arize AX
    • auto-instrumentation
  • Why it matters: Provides the practical implementation steps required to collect execution data from an agent application.

Error Analysis and Looking at Your Data

  • Explanation: The importance of reading traces, conducting error analysis, and categorizing failures before writing any evals.
  • Key claims:
    • Reading a dozen traces end-to-end is the most important practice in agent development.
    • 'The response was wrong' is not actionable; you must ask why and categorize by root cause (retrieval failure, reasoning error, hallucination, scope violation).
  • Examples:
    • Reviewing financial analyst agent runs for Apple, Tesla, and Nvidia to spot missing budget breakdowns or unverified private company data.
  • Terminology:
    • error analysis
    • open coding
    • axial coding
    • root cause analysis
  • Why it matters: Bridges raw trace data to actionable engineering insights by identifying specific failure modes.

Building and Running Code Evals

  • Explanation: Writing simple deterministic code evaluators in Python to check specific constraints like ticker symbol mentions.
  • Key claims:
    • Code evals provide instant, free, deterministic checks for format, structure, constraints, and required fields.
    • Grade the outcome, not the path; don't punish agents for taking a creative or unexpected path to the correct answer.
  • Examples:
    • Writing a Python evaluator to check if a financial report mentions the required stock ticker.
  • Terminology:
    • code evaluator
    • deterministic evaluation
    • evaluation result
    • suppress tracing
  • Why it matters: Shows how to implement fast, cheap programmatic quality gates into the evaluation pipeline.

Building LLM-as-a-Judge Evals and Rubrics

  • Explanation: Implementing semantic evaluations using LLM judges, covering correctness and faithfulness, structuring rubrics with XML tags, and managing tradeoffs.
  • Key claims:
    • An LLM judge rubric should have four parts: define the judge's role, define explicit pass/fail criteria, label data with XML tags, and define output choices outside the prompt.
    • Include labeled examples of good and bad outputs in your rubric to drastically improve judge consistency.
    • Chain-of-thought prompting (asking the judge to explain its reasoning before scoring) measurably improves evaluation accuracy.
  • Examples:
    • Using Built-In Correctness and Faithfulness evaluators with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as a judge.
  • Terminology:
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • rubric
    • faithfulness
    • correctness
    • XML tags
    • chain-of-thought
  • Why it matters: Enables evaluation of complex semantic attributes like adherence to source documents and actionability.

Meta-Evaluation: Testing Your Tests

  • Explanation: Evaluating the evaluator by comparing LLM judge predictions against human annotations to measure agreement, precision, and recall.
  • Key claims:
    • Your judge is a classifier that makes predictions (pass/fail or actionable/not actionable) that can be compared against human ground truth.
    • Human inter-rater reliability is often low (0.2–0.3 Cohen's Kappa); if your judge is more consistent than humans, that's a win.
    • When judges disagree with humans, read explanations to uncover ambiguity in your rubric.
  • Examples:
    • Calculating agreement rate between human annotations and classification evaluator scores in a pandas DataFrame.
  • Terminology:
    • meta-evaluation
    • confusion matrix
    • precision
    • recall
    • inter-rater reliability
  • Why it matters: Ensures that the evaluation suite itself is trustworthy and correctly calibrated.

The Eval-Iterate Cycle and Automated Prompt Improvement

  • Explanation: Using experiments, golden datasets, and coding agents to automatically improve agent prompts based on evaluation failure explanations.
  • Key claims:
    • Save failing production or test traces as a regression dataset to test prompt improvements systematically.
    • Feed failing trace explanations back into a coding agent or LLM to automatically rewrite and improve prompt templates.
    • The impact hierarchy for improvements is: data quality fixes first, prompting improvements second, model selection third, and hyperparameter tuning lowest.
  • Examples:
    • Exporting failing traces from Arize AX, saving them as a dataset named 'aie-financial-demo-fails', and running an experiment with improved prompts.
  • Terminology:
    • eval-driven development
    • golden dataset
    • regression test set
    • impact hierarchy
    • experiments
  • Why it matters: Completes the software development lifecycle loop for AI, turning production failures into automated regression tests.

Key Points

Treat Evals as Infrastructure

  • Explanation: Evaluations should not be an afterthought; they must be treated with the same rigor and systematic integration as unit tests in traditional software engineering.
  • Evidence: Real-world engineering teams at Descript, Bolt, and Anthropic followed the exact arc of shipping on vibes, realizing it didn't scale, and building evals.
  • Practical implication: Establish telemetry and evaluation loops early in the development process rather than trying to retrofit testing after production deployment.

Grade the Outcome, Not the Path

  • Explanation: When evaluating AI agents that perform multi-step reasoning and tool calls, grading intermediate trajectories rigidly punishes creative and valid problem-solving paths.
  • Evidence: Discussion of multi-turn customer service benchmarks where agents find valid alternative execution paths that rigid trajectory testing marks as failures.

  • Explanation: When iterating to improve agent performance, fixing knowledge base and retrieval data quality yields significantly higher returns than prompt tweaks or model switching.

  • Components:
    • Automated code evals (catches format and syntax issues)
    • LLM-as-a-judge reviews (catches semantic and reasoning gaps)
    • Manual transcript reviews / early access programs (catches novel failures)
    • Production monitoring, A/B testing, and user feedback (catches edge cases in production)
  • When to use: When designing an end-to-end quality assurance strategy for production AI applications.

  • How it works: A continuous feedback loop for AI software development that mirrors traditional CI/CD pipelines.
  • Components:
    • Find failures via tracing
    • Read explanations via error analysis
    • Fix prompts or data
    • Run experiments against test datasets
    • Repeat
  • When to use: During the development, debugging, and maintenance phases of building AI agents.

  • How it works: Prioritization framework for where to invest engineering resources when optimizing AI agent performance.
  • Components:
    • Data quality fixes (highest impact)
    • Prompting improvements
    • Model selection
    • Hyperparameter tuning (lowest impact)
  • When to use: When deciding what part of an AI system to refactor or tune following evaluation failures.

An agent tasked with finding financial data on Tesla searched the web, retrieved information on an 18th-century inventor named Tesla, and wrote a polished report about him.

  • Illustrates: Cascading failures in agent workflows where bad retrieval leads to bad reasoning and confident hallucinations.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Laurie Voss
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Evaluating and shipping production-ready AI agents using observability, tracing, code evaluations, LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, datasets, experiments, and meta-evaluation.
- **Purpose**: To educate AI engineers on how to build, trace, evaluate, and systematically improve LLM-based AI agents using structured testing, evaluation rubrics, and observability tooling.
Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, presents a comprehensive 101 workshop on moving AI agents from casual 'vibe checks' to reliable production systems. He explains why standard software unit tests and manual reviews fail for non-deterministic AI outputs, introducing a rigorous framework of OpenTelemetry tracing (via Arize AX), code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, golden datasets, error analysis, and meta-evaluation to iteratively improve agent prompts and codebases.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and Agenda
- **Explanation**: Introduction of the speaker, background, and the core agenda covering evals, tracing in Arize AX, building AI agents with the Claude Agent SDK, error analysis, code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, meta-evaluation, and dataset/experiment iteration loops.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents make evaluation much harder than single-LLM applications due to cascading errors and multi-step tool calls.
  - Most teams ship AI features based on vague vibe checks, which fails when models encounter new inputs.
- **Examples**:
  - Mention of building a financial analysis chatbot agent using the Claude Agent SDK.
- **Terminology**:
  - Arize AX
  - Claude Agent SDK
  - evals
  - traces
  - spans
- **Why it matters**: Establishes why traditional testing methods are insufficient for AI applications and sets the framework for the workshop.
### What are Evals and Why You Need Them (The Vibes Problem)
- **Explanation**: Discussion of the limitations of manual vibe checks and unit tests for LLM applications, explaining why traces are logs for AI and evals are tests for AI.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traces are logs for AI; evals are tests for AI.
  - Without evals, changing a prompt to fix one tone issue can silently hallucinate product features elsewhere.
  - Manual human review does not scale, doesn't catch regressions, and doesn't run in CI.
- **Examples**:
  - Changing system prompts and breaking unexpected parts of an application.
- **Terminology**:
  - vibes problem
  - traces
  - spans
  - evals
  - regression test
- **Why it matters**: Explains the foundational mental model needed to transition from prototyping to engineering production AI.
### Two Types of Evals: Code Evals vs. LLM-as-a-Judge Evals
- **Explanation**: Comparison of code-based deterministic checks versus semantic LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, highlighting their pros, cons, and appropriate use cases.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code evals are deterministic, free, fast, and reproducible like unit tests, but can be brittle.
  - LLM-as-a-judge evals use a second LLM to grade outputs against a rubric, handling meaning and semantics rather than just strings.
  - LLM judges cost money, are non-deterministic, and require calibration against human judgment.
- **Examples**:
  - Code eval checking if output parses as JSON or contains a ticker symbol.
  - LLM judge checking faithfulness or tone.
- **Terminology**:
  - code evals
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - rubric
  - deterministic
- **Why it matters**: Helps engineers choose the right evaluation mechanism depending on whether the test is syntactic or semantic.
### Why Agents Make Evaluation Harder
- **Explanation**: Analysis of multi-agent and multi-turn agent execution complexity, tool calls, and cascading errors.
- **Key claims**:
  - Single LLM calls have simple input-output pairs, but agents make a series of tool calls and reasoning steps.
  - Errors cascade across steps: bad retrieval leads to bad reasoning, leading to confidently wrong output.
  - Multi-agent handoffs add another layer where triage and specialist routing can fail.
- **Examples**:
  - Agent searching the web for Tesla, finding info on an 18th-century inventor instead, and writing a polished report about them.
- **Terminology**:
  - cascading failures
  - multi-agent complexity
  - tool calls
  - hallucination
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates why monitoring intermediate agent steps (spans) is essential for debugging agent workflows.
### Setting Up Tracing with Arize AX
- **Explanation**: Demonstration of setting up OpenTelemetry tracing and OpenInference instrumentation with the Claude Agent SDK to capture raw data for evaluations.
- **Key claims**:
  - You can't evaluate what you can't observe; observability comes before evaluation.
  - Auto-instrumentation via OpenInference captures prompt text, completions, token counts, model names, and tool invocations with just two lines of code.
- **Examples**:
  - Code snippet registering tracer provider with Arize AX using space ID and API key.
- **Terminology**:
  - OpenTelemetry
  - OpenInference
  - tracing
  - Arize AX
  - auto-instrumentation
- **Why it matters**: Provides the practical implementation steps required to collect execution data from an agent application.
### Error Analysis and Looking at Your Data
- **Explanation**: The importance of reading traces, conducting error analysis, and categorizing failures before writing any evals.
- **Key claims**:
  - Reading a dozen traces end-to-end is the most important practice in agent development.
  - 'The response was wrong' is not actionable; you must ask why and categorize by root cause (retrieval failure, reasoning error, hallucination, scope violation).
- **Examples**:
  - Reviewing financial analyst agent runs for Apple, Tesla, and Nvidia to spot missing budget breakdowns or unverified private company data.
- **Terminology**:
  - error analysis
  - open coding
  - axial coding
  - root cause analysis
- **Why it matters**: Bridges raw trace data to actionable engineering insights by identifying specific failure modes.
### Building and Running Code Evals
- **Explanation**: Writing simple deterministic code evaluators in Python to check specific constraints like ticker symbol mentions.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code evals provide instant, free, deterministic checks for format, structure, constraints, and required fields.
  - Grade the outcome, not the path; don't punish agents for taking a creative or unexpected path to the correct answer.
- **Examples**:
  - Writing a Python evaluator to check if a financial report mentions the required stock ticker.
- **Terminology**:
  - code evaluator
  - deterministic evaluation
  - evaluation result
  - suppress tracing
- **Why it matters**: Shows how to implement fast, cheap programmatic quality gates into the evaluation pipeline.
### Building LLM-as-a-Judge Evals and Rubrics
- **Explanation**: Implementing semantic evaluations using LLM judges, covering correctness and faithfulness, structuring rubrics with XML tags, and managing tradeoffs.
- **Key claims**:
  - An LLM judge rubric should have four parts: define the judge's role, define explicit pass/fail criteria, label data with XML tags, and define output choices outside the prompt.
  - Include labeled examples of good and bad outputs in your rubric to drastically improve judge consistency.
  - Chain-of-thought prompting (asking the judge to explain its reasoning before scoring) measurably improves evaluation accuracy.
- **Examples**:
  - Using Built-In Correctness and Faithfulness evaluators with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as a judge.
- **Terminology**:
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - rubric
  - faithfulness
  - correctness
  - XML tags
  - chain-of-thought
- **Why it matters**: Enables evaluation of complex semantic attributes like adherence to source documents and actionability.
### Meta-Evaluation: Testing Your Tests
- **Explanation**: Evaluating the evaluator by comparing LLM judge predictions against human annotations to measure agreement, precision, and recall.
- **Key claims**:
  - Your judge is a classifier that makes predictions (pass/fail or actionable/not actionable) that can be compared against human ground truth.
  - Human inter-rater reliability is often low (0.2–0.3 Cohen's Kappa); if your judge is more consistent than humans, that's a win.
  - When judges disagree with humans, read explanations to uncover ambiguity in your rubric.
- **Examples**:
  - Calculating agreement rate between human annotations and classification evaluator scores in a pandas DataFrame.
- **Terminology**:
  - meta-evaluation
  - confusion matrix
  - precision
  - recall
  - inter-rater reliability
- **Why it matters**: Ensures that the evaluation suite itself is trustworthy and correctly calibrated.
### The Eval-Iterate Cycle and Automated Prompt Improvement
- **Explanation**: Using experiments, golden datasets, and coding agents to automatically improve agent prompts based on evaluation failure explanations.
- **Key claims**:
  - Save failing production or test traces as a regression dataset to test prompt improvements systematically.
  - Feed failing trace explanations back into a coding agent or LLM to automatically rewrite and improve prompt templates.
  - The impact hierarchy for improvements is: data quality fixes first, prompting improvements second, model selection third, and hyperparameter tuning lowest.
- **Examples**:

  - regression test set
